1114.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1114.hook: night six: in Bengal the drums start, and the goddess is welcomed as a married daughter coming home with her children
1114.howItsDone: In Bengal, Durga Puja centers on clay images of Durga with Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesha and Kartikeya in pandals, and songs welcome her as Uma, a daughter visiting her parents; where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night honors Katyayani.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night five of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Skandamata, a mother with her child, and a staircase of dolls.
screen: `THE POWER THAT HOLDS YOU.` · `NIGHT SIX.`

segments.voice: Drums. Big ones, slung on the shoulder, beaten with two sticks, and the sound carries down the lane. In Kolkata and across Bengal, around this point in the nights, Durga Puja gets under way. Inside a decorated tent called a pandal stands a clay goddess with many arms, a lion at her feet and the buffalo demon under her spear. But look at who's with her: Lakshmi on one side, Saraswati on the other, Ganesha, Kartikeya on his peacock. She hasn't come alone. She's brought the children. Tonight, the sixth name in the Kavacha's list, Katyayani, and in Bengal, a homecoming.
screen: `DRUMS DOWN THE LANE.` → `A GODDESS WITH HER CHILDREN.` → `SIXTH NIGHT: KATYAYANI.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Katyayani is sixth in the Kavacha's list, and there's a story people tell about it: that she appeared in the hermitage of a sage called Katyayana, and took his name the way a daughter takes her father's. In the stories of the nine forms, she's the warrior form, the one who goes out to meet the buffalo demon. Now Bengal, where the goddess has another name, Uma, and another story wrapped around the battle; day ninety-four touched it. Uma is the daughter of the mountain king, Himalaya, married far away to Shiva on Mount Kailash. Once a year, the songs say, she comes home to her parents' house for a few days, and brings her children with her. Her mother has been waiting at the door all year. Bengali agamani songs are sung in the mother's voice: is my Uma coming? Is she thin? Is her husband treating her well? So the festival holds two pictures at once. On the altar, the goddess with many arms, killing a demon. In the songs, a married daughter on a visit, and a mother who can't stop fussing over her. Neither picture cancels the other. That's the sixth lesson: the goddess who protects the universe is also somebody's child, coming home. And the homecoming has an end. When the festival is over she leaves, and the leaving is part of it. People say goodbye to her the way you'd say goodbye to a daughter at the station.
screen: `KATYAYANI, THE SIXTH NAME.` · `UMA, DAUGHTER OF THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A MOTHER WAITING AT THE DOOR.` · `WARRIOR AND DAUGHTER AT ONCE.` · then, large: `SHE IS COMING HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love who lives far away, or whom you don't see often enough, and picture them walking up to your door; be the mother in the songs for a minute: are they eating, are they all right? Then let the worry soften into welcome, and just be glad they exist. If you pray, you can hold them before the goddess, or before God, in whatever words you use.

1115.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1115.hook: night seven: a dark, fearsome form of the goddess arrives on the night Saraswati's nights begin, and in some homes the books go to rest
1115.howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in South India, books, pens and instruments are placed before Saraswati in the last days of Navaratri and not used until Vijayadashami; where the nine forms are kept, the seventh night honors Kalaratri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night six of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Katyayani, and Uma coming home to a mother waiting at the door.
screen: `SHE IS COMING HOME.` · `NIGHT SEVEN.`

segments.voice: A schoolbook, a pen, a harmonium, a child's slate. In some homes, around this point in Navaratri, they're stacked together in front of an image of Saraswati, the goddess of learning, music and speech, and decorated with a little sandal paste and a flower. Then nobody touches them: no homework from those books, no practice on that instrument, until the festival is over. In the three-by-three way of keeping the festival, Saraswati's nights begin about now. But the seventh name in the Kavacha's list is not gentle at all.
screen: `BOOKS STACKED BEFORE SARASWATI.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES THEM.` → `THE SEVENTH NAME IS NOT GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Her name is Kalaratri. You can hear the word ratri in it, night, the same word that's in Navaratri. In paintings of this night she's black as a moonless sky, hair loose and wild, breath like fire, sometimes riding a donkey. Nothing about her is there to reassure you. And yet devotees who keep the nine forms give her a second name, Shubhankari, the one who does good. The fearsome form is the protecting one. So here's the odd thing about the order. On the very night the learning nights begin, the goddess comes as night itself. Why put them together? One way to read it: real learning starts where you're scared. The thing you avoid looking at, the subject you're sure you're bad at, the conversation you keep putting off. Kalaratri is the form that walks straight into the dark, and Saraswati is the clarity on the other side. Then the books. Setting them down before Saraswati says something simple: knowledge isn't only a tool you pick up and use. It's a gift you can bow to. For a few days the pens and books and instruments rest, the way a field rests, and the people who use them rest too. When the festival is over they're picked up again with a blessing, and in some places little children write their first letters that day. So night seven teaches a pair. Face the dark, and then honor what helps you see.
screen: `KALARATRI: NIGHT IN HER NAME.` · `FEARSOME, AND SHE DOES GOOD.` · `LEARNING STARTS WHERE YOU'RE SCARED.` · `BOOKS AT REST, PICKED UP AS A GIFT.` · then, large: `FACE THE DARK. HONOR WHAT HELPS YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the dark behind your eyelids be just what it is; then turn toward one thing you've been afraid to learn or to look at, a subject, a skill, a conversation, and for a few breaths simply stop looking away from it, without solving it. Let one small first step toward it come to mind, a question you could ask, a page you could read. If you pray, you can ask Saraswati, or God, for clarity, in words you already know.

1116.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1116.hook: night eight: Mahagauri, the bright one, and in some homes young girls are welcomed in, their feet washed, and fed as the goddess
1116.howItsDone: In parts of North India, families keep kanya puja (kanjak) on the eighth or ninth day of Navaratri, washing the feet of young girls, feeding them puri, halwa and chickpeas, and giving them small gifts; where the nine forms are kept, the eighth night honors Mahagauri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night seven of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Kalaratri, the goddess as night, and the books set down before Saraswati.
screen: `FACE THE DARK. HONOR WHAT HELPS YOU SEE.` · `NIGHT EIGHT.`

segments.voice: The doorbell rings, and it's the girls from down the street, a little shy, in their best clothes. Inside, the grown-ups have been cooking since early: puris, a sweet semolina halwa, spiced chickpeas. The girls sit in a row. An aunt kneels and washes their feet, dabs a red mark on each forehead, ties a red thread on each wrist. They're served first, before anyone else eats, and they leave with a small gift. In parts of North India this is kanya puja, or kanjak, kept on the eighth or ninth day. For a morning, the goddess is the girl next door.
screen: `THE GIRLS FROM DOWN THE STREET.` → `FEET WASHED, SERVED FIRST.` → `THE GODDESS NEXT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The eighth name in the Kavacha's list is Mahagauri. It means the great Gauri, and Gauri is a name of Parvati, the bright one. On this night she's shown dressed in white, calm, shining. There's a story people tell about it. Parvati did hard austerities for a long time to win Shiva, out in the sun and the rain, until her body was darkened with dust and weather. When Shiva finally accepted her, he washed her with the water of the Ganga, and she came out shining. So the bright form is what's left after long effort, washed clean. Now hold that next to the morning with the girls. Usually it's the children who touch the feet of their elders, and the children who wait to be served. In kanya puja the elders wash the children's feet. The girls eat first, and the aunts and grandmothers serve them. The idea behind it is plain: the goddess the house has honored for eight nights is honored in the girls themselves. Not as a symbol on a shelf, but as someone sitting at your table, swinging her feet because the chair is too high. Put the two together and night eight teaches something about seeing. After all the effort of the earlier nights, the curriculum asks you to look at an ordinary person, a young person, someone you might overlook, and see something shining there. Mahagauri is brightness after effort. Kanya puja is learning to see that brightness in a child.
screen: `MAHAGAURI, THE GREAT BRIGHT ONE.` · `WASHED CLEAN AFTER LONG EFFORT.` · `THE ELDERS WASH THE GIRLS' FEET.` · `THE GODDESS AT YOUR TABLE.` · then, large: `SEE THE BRIGHTNESS IN A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child or a young person you know, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, your own, and see their face. Instead of the usual thoughts, homework, screen time, behavior, look at them the way the aunts look at the girls at kanya puja: as someone worth serving, with something bright in them. If you pray, you can hold them before the goddess, or before God, in your own words.

1117.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1117.hook: night nine: auto-rickshaws wear garlands, a mechanic puts a flower on his wrench, and the last name in the list is the giver of accomplishment
1117.howItsDone: In parts of South India, Ayudha Puja on the ninth day of Navaratri honors tools, vehicles, machines and instruments, which are cleaned, decorated and rested; where the nine forms are kept, the ninth night honors Siddhidatri, and the next day is Vijayadashami.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night eight of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Mahagauri, and girls served first at the table. Tonight, the last night.
screen: `SEE THE BRIGHTNESS IN A CHILD.` · `NIGHT NINE.`

segments.voice: An auto-rickshaw parked outside a temple, with a garland of marigolds across its windshield and a smear of turmeric on the bumper. A mechanic's shop where the wrenches have been wiped clean, laid in a row and given a flower each. A tailor's sewing machine with a red dot on it. A laptop, closed, with a sprig of something green on the lid. In parts of South India, the ninth day of Navaratri is Ayudha Puja, the worship of tools. Where it's kept, the tools aren't worked with today. They're cleaned, thanked and honored.
screen: `A GARLAND ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A FLOWER ON EACH WRENCH.` → `TOOLS CLEANED AND HONORED.`

segments.voice: And the ninth name in the Kavacha's list, the last one, is Siddhidatri, the giver of siddhi: accomplishment, the power to bring a thing to completion. On this night she's shown seated on a lotus, calm. Fitting, for a last night. Look back. In the three-by-three way of keeping the nights, Durga's nights cleared the road, Lakshmi's filled the house, and Saraswati's turned toward knowing. In the nine forms, the goddess was a daughter of the mountain, a smile that made a world, a mother with her child, a warrior named for a sage's hermitage, night itself, the bright one washed clean. And now she gives accomplishment. Ayudha Puja says where accomplishment actually comes from: the work of your hands, and the tools you do it with. The wrench, the sewing machine, the pen, the stove. Honoring them for a day says the ordinary instruments of a life are worth bowing to. And remember night one. Near the end of the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess herself speaks of the great worship offered to her in autumn, and says that whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles by her grace. So the curriculum ends where it began, bound to the book. And this part of the year closes. It began with the Devi Mahatmya read whole, then the goddesses as characters, Shakti as a philosophy, the Sri Sukta, the names of Lalita, and these nine nights. Tomorrow the year turns to Shiva, and to the Shiva Purana.
screen: `SIDDHIDATRI, GIVER OF ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `CLEAR, FILL, KNOW, FINISH.` · `HONOR THE TOOLS OF YOUR HANDS.` · `THE AUTUMN WORSHIP AND THE BOOK.` · then, large: `THE GODDESS'S PART, COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: One by one, bring to mind the things your hands use to get through a day, keys, a phone, a pan, a pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a broom, and give each a moment of thanks, the way the mechanic gives each wrench a flower. Then let the hands themselves come to mind, resting in your lap; they're tools too. If you pray, you can offer the work of your hands to the goddess, or to God, in your own words.

1118.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1118.hook: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greater when a pillar of fire splits the sky between them
1118.howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus worship Shiva in the form of the linga in temples and homes, and the story of the endless pillar of fire is told and carved in temples as the appearance of the linga, Lingodbhava; it is also linked to Maha Shivaratri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum, and the goddess's part of the year, with tools resting under flowers. Today the year turns to Shiva.
screen: `THE DEVI, COMPLETE.` · `NOW: SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going. The argument gets hot. Then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears, blazing, going up past where they can see and down past where they can see. No top in sight, and no bottom. Both gods stop mid-sentence. You heard this on Shivaratri, back on day ninety; today it comes from the Shiva Purana itself.
screen: `TWO GODS ARGUING.` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana is a big book of stories about Shiva, his worship and the people around him. It presents itself as told aloud: a storyteller named Suta recounting it to a gathering of sages. The path takes selections, not the whole. The two gods agree on a test: whoever finds the end of this thing wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go a very long way. Vishnu finds no bottom, and finally comes back and says so: he couldn't find the end. Brahma finds no top. But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back, says he reached the top, and brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it. He honors Vishnu for telling the truth and rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship. Here's what makes it worth carrying. The point isn't who won. Nobody found the end. For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar: something that can't be measured from either side. And the one who comes out well is the one who admitted it: I couldn't find the end. Before something that big, the story honors the honest answer, and rebukes the one who pretended to have it figured out.

1119.hook: Daksha holds a great sacrifice and leaves out one guest, his own son-in-law Shiva, and his daughter Sati decides to go anyway
1119.howItsDone: Hindus tell the story of Sati and Daksha's sacrifice in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas; Shaiva temples honor Virabhadra, and Sati's story is linked to the shakti pithas, places sacred to the goddess.

screen: `I COULDN'T FIND THE END.` · `A SECOND SELECTION.`

segments.voice: From the slopes of Kailash, Sati sees them go by in the sky: gods and their wives, dressed for a celebration, all heading the same way. They're going to her father's house. Daksha, her father, is holding a great sacrifice, a yajna, and the guests are streaming in. Everyone, it seems, except Sati and her husband. Daksha has left out his own son-in-law, Shiva. Sati turns to her husband and says she wants to go. A family quarrel that shakes the world.
screen: `GUESTS IN THE SKY.` → `EVERYONE BUT SHIVA.` → `SATI WANTS TO GO.`

segments.voice: The grudge is old. At an earlier gathering of the gods, Daksha walked in and the others rose to honor him, but Shiva stayed seated. Daksha took it as an insult. To him, Shiva was an embarrassment of a son-in-law: smeared with ash, wandering cremation grounds, no fine house. Shiva tells Sati plainly that going is a bad idea: to go where you haven't been invited brings dishonor, and her father means to insult them. But it's her father's house; surely her family won't turn her away. So she goes, and it's worse than Shiva said. There's no portion set aside for Shiva at all. Her father greets her coldly and speaks of her husband with contempt in front of everyone. Sati won't hear it. She rebukes her father before the gods, and then, the story says, she gives up her body by the power of her own yoga, rather than live as the daughter of the man who mocked Shiva. When word reaches Shiva, his grief becomes fury. From his matted hair he brings out Virabhadra, a terrible warrior, who storms the sacrifice and wrecks it. Daksha is killed. When the gods beg, Shiva relents, and Daksha is brought back to life with the head of a goat: a proud man, given a humbler face and a second chance. The story holds a lot of feeling, a daughter's loyalty, a husband's grief, a father's pride, and it treats contempt as no small thing: here, mockery brings down a great sacrifice. 1120.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1120.hook: spring arrives on Shiva's mountain out of season, and Kama, the god of desire, takes aim at the god who is deep in meditation
1120.howItsDone: Hindus tell the burning of Kama in the Shiva Purana and in poetry and dance; Shiva is often shown with a third eye on his forehead, and in some places the story is remembered at Holi or in spring festivals.

screen: `A FAMILY QUARREL SHAKES THE WORLD.` · `A THIRD SELECTION.`

segments.voice: On a frozen mountainside, the snow starts to melt. Out of season, trees burst into flower. Bees show up, a cuckoo sings, the breeze turns warm and sweet. Every living thing on the mountain feels it, except one. Under a tree, Shiva sits in meditation, perfectly still, eyes closed, as if spring were somebody else's business. Behind a bush, with a bow made of sugarcane and arrows tipped with flowers, crouches Kama, the god of desire. He's been sent on a mission, and he's nervous.
screen: `SPRING, OUT OF SEASON.` → `SHIVA, PERFECTLY STILL.` → `KAMA TAKES AIM.`

segments.voice: Here's why he's there. Since Sati gave up her body, Shiva has withdrawn into meditation. Sati has been born again as Parvati, the daughter of the mountain king, and she comes every day to serve him: flowers, water, a clean place to sit. He doesn't look up. Meanwhile a demon named Taraka has a boon, and in the Shiva Purana only a son of Shiva can defeat him. So the gods need Shiva to marry, and Shiva is busy being still. Indra, king of the gods, sends Kama, and Spring with him. Desire will do what persuasion can't. Kama waits for his moment, Parvati standing near, and lets an arrow fly. For a moment it works. Shiva's mind stirs; he opens his eyes and looks at Parvati. Then he catches himself, looks for the cause, and sees Kama with his bow. Fire bursts from Shiva's third eye, and Kama is burned to ash on the spot. You met this at Holi, on day ninety-six, and its far end in a hymn to the goddess; here is how the book tells it. Rati, Kama's wife, falls weeping beside the ashes, and in the story she's promised her husband will live again. Shiva leaves; Parvati goes home. Notice what this teaches by failing. Help from outside, spring, flowers, an arrow, couldn't win Shiva; desire forced in burned up. Whatever wins him will have to come from Parvati herself. That closes a week full of fire: Navaratri's last nights, the honest god at the pillar of flame, Sati at the sacrifice, and now the third eye.
screen: `PARVATI SERVES; SHIVA IS STILL.` · `THE GODS SEND DESIRE.` · `THE THIRD EYE OPENS.` · `IT CAN'T BE FORCED FROM OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `KAMA, BURNED TO ASH.`

segments.voice: Sit as still as you comfortably can, and sooner or later a want will show up: to check your phone, to eat, to be somewhere else. Don't fight it or follow it; notice it, watch it rise and fall like spring around a still figure under a tree, and come back to the breath. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as you come back.
